text: The medulla is continuous above with:
explanation: Based on your texts, the medulla 'is continuous above with the pons'. (Page 48)

text: The ventral spinocerebellar tract crosses:
explanation: Based on your texts, the ascending pathway for the ventral spinocerebellar tract is described as 'Fibers cross medial line'. The text also mentions the 'Decussation of ventral spino-cerebellar tract' in the midbrain. (Pages 38, 74)

text: Which is the length of medulla oblongata?
explanation: Based on your texts, the medulla is 'Approximately 3 cm in length'. (Page 48)

text: The pyramids of the medulla represent:
explanation: Based on your texts, the pyramids are an 'elevation produced by underlying corticospinal tract'. (Page 49)

text: Motor decussation occurs in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Lower medulla' (which is part of the closed medulla) 'contains motor decussation of pyramidal tract'. (Page 52)

text: Nervous tissue is mainly composed of:
explanation: Based on your texts, nervous tissue is defined as one of the four basic tissues and consists of 'nerve cells (neurons) and supporting cells (neuroglia)'. (Page 5)

text: Ganglia are:
options: Collections of nerve cell bodies outside CNS
explanation: Based on your texts, ganglia are explicitly defined as a 'collection of nerve cell bodies outside the central nervous system' and as 'small aggregates of nerve cells outside of the CNS'. (Pages 5, 12)

text: Neurons are considered:
options: Structural and functional unit of nervous tissue
Dividing stem cells of nervous tissue
explanation: Based on your texts, the neuron is defined as the 'structural and functional unit of nervous tissue'. (Page 5)

text: Nissl granules are absent from:
explanation: Based on your texts, Nissl granules are described as being present in the cell body and dendrites, but 'it is absent from the axon and axon hillock'. (Page 6)

text: Axon terminals are called:
explanation: Based on your texts, the axon is described to 'end in several branches called telodendria'. (Page 8)

text: Pseudo unipolar neurons are typically found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the site for pseudounipolar neurons is listed as 'Spinal sensory ganglia'. (Page 9)

text: True unipolar neurons are located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, true unipolar neurons are described as being 'located in mesenchephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve'. (Page 9)

text: Bipolar neurons are commonly associated with:
explanation: Based on your texts, the site for bipolar neurons is listed as 'Neurons in special sense organs e.g. olfactory epithelium'. (Page 9)

text: Multipolar neurons are:
options: Found only in spinal sensory ganglia
The most common neurons in brain and spinal cord
explanation: Based on your texts, multipolar neurons are described as being present in 'Most of the neurons in the brain and spinal cord'. (Page 10)

text: Purkinje cells of cerebellum are:
explanation: Based on your texts, Purkinje cells of the cerebellar cortex are listed as an example of multipolar neurons that have a 'Pyriform shape'. (Page 10)

text: Golgi type I neurons are characterized by:
explanation: Based on your texts, Golgi type I neurons are characterized by a 'long axon' and 'form long tracts in the brain and spinal cord'. (Page 11)

text: Golgi type II neurons are mainly found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the site for Golgi type II neurons is described as 'very numerous in cerebral and cerebellar cortex and in the retina'. (Page 11)

text: The supportive cells surrounding ganglionic perikarya are:
explanation: Based on your texts, satellite cells are the supportive cells in the PNS that 'surround the neuronal cell bodies of ganglia (spinal and autonomic ganglia)'. (Page 19)

text: Myelinated fibers with neurolemma are found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, one of the types of nerve fibers listed is 'Myelinated with neurolemma', which are identified as the 'nerve fibers of PNS'. (Page 14)

text: Myelinated fibers without neurolemma occur in:
explanation: Based on your texts, a type of nerve fiber listed is 'Myelinated without neurolemma-nerve fibers of CNS'. (Page 14)

text: Unmyelinated fibers with neurolemma are found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, one of the types of nerve fibers listed is 'Unmyelinated with neurolemma-Autonomic ganglia'. (Page 14)

text: Naked nerve fibers are:
explanation: Based on your texts, a 'naked nerve fiber' is defined as being 'Unmyelinated without neurolemma' and is found at the 'origin and termination of nerve fiber'. (Page 14)

text: The insulating material of a nerve fiber is:
explanation: Based on your texts, it is stated that 'myelin which consists of phospholipids acts as an insulator'. (Page 14)

text: In PNS, the myelin sheath is formed by:
explanation: Based on your texts, for myelination in the PNS, 'the myelin sheath is an insulation formed by Schwann cells around axons'. (Page 14)

text: The last loose wrap of Schwann cell plasma membrane containing nucleus & cytoplasm is called:
explanation: Based on your texts, the neurolemma is defined as 'the last wrapping of the plasma membrane of the Schwann cell, it is loose and contains the nucleus, cytoplasm, and organelles of the Schwann cell'. (Page 14)

text: The uninsulated gaps between Schwann cells along an axon are:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Spaces... between adjacent Schwann cells, leaving uninsulated areas' are called 'neurofibril nodes (nodes of Ranvier)'. (Page 14)

text: Mesaxon refers to:
options: Point of contact between Schwann cell membrane and axon
explanation: Based on your texts, the Mesaxon is defined as 'the point of contact between the cell membrane of the Schwann cell and the axon'. (Pages 14-15)

text: In CNS, myelin is formed by:
explanation: Based on your texts, for myelination in the CNS, 'the axons of neurons are insulated by oligodendrocytes'. (Page 15)

text: One oligodendrocyte can myelinate:
explanation: Based on your texts, it is stated that 'Many axons may be myelinated by multiple processes from a single oligodendrocyte'. (Page 15)

text: Unmyelinated axons in CNS are supported by:
explanation: Based on your texts, it is noted that 'Unmyelinated nerve in CNS supported by astrocytes'. (Page 15)

text: In routine H&E stained sections, myelin appears as:
explanation: Based on your texts, in H&E sections, the lipid-rich myelin sheath 'dissolves during staining' and nerve fibers appear 'surrounded by a pale unstained area (the site of myelin)'. (Page 16)

text: The outermost connective tissue sheath of a peripheral nerve is:
explanation: Based on your texts, the epineurium is the 'sheath of connective tissue surrounding a peripheral nerve', making it the outermost layer. (Page 16)

text: Perineurium encloses:
explanation: Based on your texts, the perineurium is the connective tissue layer that 'enclosed each bundle or fascicle of nerve fibers'. (Page 16)

text: Endoneurium lies:
explanation: Based on your texts, the endoneurium consists of delicate fibers that 'lie between individual nerve fibers within each fascicle'. (Page 16)

text: In osmium tetroxide staining, myelin sheath appears:
explanation: Based on your texts, in sections stained with 'osmic acid (osmium tetroxide), lipid is stained black'. (Page 16)

text: Axoplasm contains all of the following except:
explanation: Based on your texts, the axoplasm is described as containing neurofilaments (neurofibrils), neurotubules, and mitochondria, but it 'does not contain Nissl substance'. (Page 8)

text: The smallest glial cells in CNS with phagocytic activity are:
explanation: Based on your texts, microglia are described as 'small spindle shaped cell' that 'possess phagocytotic properties'. (Page 18)

text: Protoplasmic astrocytes are mainly located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, protoplasmic astrocytes 'are found mainly in the gray matter'. (Page 19)

text: Fibrous astrocytes are mainly located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, fibrous astrocytes 'occur mainly in white matter'. (Page 19)

text: Ependymal cells line:
options: Ventricles of brain and central canal of spinal cord
explanation: Based on your texts, ependymal cells are described as lining 'the central canal of the spinal cord and ventricles of the brain'. (Page 20)

text: Satellite cells in PNS surround:
explanation: Based on your texts, satellite cells are found in the PNS and 'surround the neuronal cell bodies of ganglia'. (Page 19)

text: A synapse with thick postsynaptic density is called:
explanation: Based on your texts, the asymmetric (type 1) synapse is defined by its 'postsynaptic protein condensation', which corresponds to a thick postsynaptic density. (Page 22)

text: A synapse between axon and dendrite is:
explanation: Based on your texts, a synapse occurring between an 'Axon and dendrite' is called 'axodendritic' (listed as 'avodendritic' in the text). (Page 22)

text: The motor end-plate is defined as:
options: A sensory ending in smooth muscle
Specialized junction where a motor axon contacts skeletal muscle fiber
explanation: Based on your texts, the motor end plate is explicitly defined as 'the specialized attachment site where a motor nerve fiber connects to the skeletal muscle fiber'. (Page 24)

text: Which nerve endings act as pain receptors in the skin?
explanation: Based on your texts, 'Naked nerve endings' are described as functioning 'as pain receptors in skin'. (Page 25)

text: Merkel's disks are located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, Merkel's disks are described as being in contact with Merkel cells located 'in the basal layer of the epidermis'. (Page 25)

text: The peritrichial plexus surrounds:
explanation: Based on your texts, the peritrichial plexus of bounet is described as 'Basket arrays naked nerve endings which spiral around the base of hair follicles'. (Page 25)

text: Neuromuscular spindle intrafusal fibers include:
options: Nuclear bag and nuclear chain fibers
explanation: Based on your texts, the two main types of intrafusal muscle fibers listed for the neuromuscular spindle are the 'Nuclear bag fiber' and the 'Nuclear chain fiber'. (Page 27)

text: The supporting cells of taste buds are called:
explanation: Based on your texts, the cell types in taste buds include ''Dark' cells', which are also referred to as '(supportive or sustentacular cells)'. (Page 30)

text: Taste buds are mainly located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, taste bud receptor cells are described as sensing stimuli 'in the oral cavity', which is where they are located. (Page 30)

text: The axons of olfactory receptor cells form the:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'axons of the [olfactory] receptor cells... are grouped into bundles to form the olfactory nerve'. (Page 30)

text: Olfactory receptor cells are:
explanation: Based on your texts, 'Olfactory epithelium receptor cells are modified bipolar neurons'. (Page 30)

text: Baroreceptors are located in:
options: Large arteries of head and neck
explanation: Based on your texts, baroreceptors are described as being located 'in the tunica adventitia of all large arteries of the head and neck'. (Page 29)

text: The outermost meningeal layer of the CNS is:
explanation: Based on your texts, the meninges are described as three layers, and 'The dura mater is the outermost layer'. (Page 32)

text: The pia mater is:
options: Delicate vascular membrane closely adherent to CNS
explanation: Based on your texts, the pia mater is described as 'very delicate and it is tightly associated [adherent] with the surface of the spinal cord and brain'. It is also noted as being 'highly vascularized'. (Pages 32, 91)

text: The fibrous extension anchoring the spinal cord is called:
explanation: Based on your texts, the spinal cord is described as 'terminating in a fibrous extension known as the filum terminale'. (Page 33)

text: The anterior horn of the spinal cord contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Anterior horn' is associated with motor functions and contains 'motor nuclei'. (Pages 34, 35)

text: The posterior horn of the spinal cord contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'posterior horn' is associated with sensory functions and contains 'sensory nuclei'. (Pages 34, 35)

text: The lateral horn is present in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the lateral horn is described as being 'in thoracic region'. (Page 34)

text: The central canal of the spinal cord contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, the central canal 'contains cerebrospinal fluid'. (Page 34)

text: The gray matter of the spinal cord is shaped like:
explanation: Based on your texts, the gray matter is described as having a 'butterfly-shape' and is also referred to as the 'butterfly (H shaped) region'. (Pages 34-35)

text: The posterior horn nucleus associated with pain and temperature is:
explanation: Based on your texts, the table on ascending tracts shows that the Lateral spinothalamic tract, which carries 'Pain & Temperature', relays in the 'SGR' (Substantia Gelatinosa of Rolando). (Page 38)

text: Clarke's nucleus is located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, Clark's nucleus (or dorsal nucleus) is listed as one of the sensory nuclei located in the 'Posterior horn'. (Page 35)

text: Rexed lamina II corresponds to:
explanation: Based on your texts, the Rexed classification lists 'Lamina II: Substantia gelatinosa of Rolando'. (Page 36)

text: Lamina IX contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, the Rexed classification lists 'Lamina IX: anterior horn (motor) cell'. (Page 36)

text: The pyramidal tracts originate mainly from:
explanation: Based on your texts, the pyramidal tracts (specifically the corticospinal tract) originate from the 'Betz cell (pyramidal) of upper part of area 4 and area 6'. (Page 36)

text: The corticospinal tract terminates in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the corticospinal tract is described as terminating at the 'anterior horn cell of spinal cord'. (Page 37)

text: The rubrospinal tract originates from:
explanation: Based on your texts, the rubrospinal tract originates from the 'Red nucleus of the mid brain'. (Page 37)

text: The tectospinal tract arises from:
explanation: Based on your texts, the tectospinal tract originates from the 'Superior tectum of the mid brain'. (Page 37)

text: At cervical level, white matter relative to gray matter is:
explanation: Based on your texts, at the cervical level, the 'gray matter [is] less than white', meaning the white matter is more. (Page 35)

text: At sacral level, gray matter relative to white matter is:
explanation: Based on your texts, at the sacral level, the 'gray matter [is] more than white'. (Page 35)

text: The lumbar region of the spinal cord in cross-section is:
options: Round, small, with thick posterior and broad anterior horns
explanation: Based on your texts, the lumbar region is described as 'round in shape and small in size' with 'thick' posterior horns and 'broad' anterior horns. (Page 45)

text: The central canal at lumbar level is:
explanation: Based on your texts, in the lumbar region, 'The central canal is in the center'. (Page 45)

text: Clark's nucleus is found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, Clark's nucleus is listed as present in the upper thoracic, lower thoracic, and lumbar regions, but it is not listed in the cervical region (Page 40). (Pages 41, 43, 45)

text: Which of the following is a short tract?
explanation: Based on your texts, Lissauer's tract is explicitly listed under the heading 'Short ascending tracts'. (Page 39)

text: Sensory decussation is due to crossing of:
explanation: Based on your texts, axons from the gracile and cuneate nuclei 'form the internal arcuate fibers which cross to opposite side forming sensory decussation'. (Page 56)

text: Fasciculus gracilis terminates in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the axons that make up the fasciculus gracilis terminate in the 'nucleus gracilis'. (Page 49)

text: Cranial nerves emerging from posterolateral sulcus of medulla include:
explanation: Based on your texts, the rootlets of the 'glossopharyngeal, vagus and cranial part of accessory' nerves emerge along the 'Posterolateral sulcus'. (Page 49)

text: The facial colliculus is produced by:
options: Abducent nucleus with looping facial fibers
explanation: Based on your texts, the facial colliculus 'overlies the nucleus of abducent nerve' and is formed because 'the fibers of the facial nerve wind around' this nucleus. (Page 57)

text: The pontocerebellar fibers connect:
options: Pons -> Cerebellum via middle cerebellar peduncle
explanation: Based on your texts, pontocerebellar fibers 'pass to contralateral cerebellum, forming middle cerebellar peduncle'. (Page 60)

text: Trapezoid body fibers are part of:
explanation: Based on your texts, the trapezoid body 'consists of transverse crossing fibers in the auditory pathway'. (Page 61)

text: Middle cerebellar peduncle connects:
explanation: Based on your texts, the table on cerebellar peduncles lists the 'Middle cerebellar peduncle' as connecting the 'Pons' to the cerebellum. (Page 86)

text: The abducent nucleus lies in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the abducent nucleus is located in the 'lower level' of the pons, and it underlies the 'facial colliculus'. (Pages 57, 61)

text: At mid-pons level, the main sensory nucleus of trigeminal deals with:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'mid-level' of the pons is the 'level of trigeminal nerve', which includes the 'Chief sensory nucleus of trigeminal'. The text associates the spinal nucleus with pain/temperature and the mesencephalic nucleus with proprioception, leaving touch as the primary modality for the chief sensory nucleus. (Pages 9, 58, 59, 61, 71)

text: The mesencephalic nucleus of trigeminal is special because:
options: Contains unipolar sensory neurons inside CNS
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'mesenchephalic nucleus of trigeminal nerve' is listed as the location for 'True unipolar neuron', which is unique for sensory neurons being located inside the CNS. (Page 9)

text: Which cranial nerves emerge at the cerebellopontine angle?
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'facial [nerve VII] - originates from the cerebellopontine angle', and the 'vestibulocochlear [nerve VIII] - originates laterally to the facial nerve' in the same area. (Page 59)

text: Inferior cerebellar peduncle connects cerebellum with:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Inferior cerebellar peduncle' is stated to 'Connects medulla to cerebellum' and is listed in a table as having its 'Connection' in the 'Medulla'. (Pages 49, 86)

text: Decussation of corticospinal tract occurs at:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'motor decussation of crossed cortico-spinal tract' occurs in the 'Lower level' of the 'closed medulla'. (Pages 52, 74)

text: Vestibular nuclei are located at:
explanation: Based on your texts, the vestibular nuclei 'are located at the pons and medulla oblongata, at the floor of the 4th ventricle'. (Page 64)

text: The trapezoid body is prominent in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the trapezoid body 'is located at the center of the lower level of the pons'. (Page 61)

text: Facial nucleus lies in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'motor nucleus of facial' is listed as a structure in the 'PONS LOWER LEVEL'. (Pages 60-61)

text: Superior olivary nucleus is part of:
explanation: Based on your texts, the superior olivary nucleus is listed with the cochlear nuclei and its fibers contribute to the trapezoid body, which is part of the 'auditory pathway'. (Pages 61, 63)

text: The corticopontine fibers terminate in:
explanation: Based on your texts, corticopontine fibers are descending fibers that travel 'via pontine nuclei', where they terminate to synapse. (Page 67)

text: The midbrain connects the pons and cerebellum with the:
explanation: Based on your texts, the midbrain 'connects the pons and cerebellum with the forebrain'. (Page 65)

text: The length of the midbrain is approximately:
explanation: Based on your texts, the midbrain measures 'around 2cm in length'. (Page 65)

text: The ventral surface of the midbrain shows:
explanation: Based on your texts, 'The ventral surface of the midbrain shows two massive cerebral peduncles'. (Page 65)

text: Which cranial nerve emerges from the medial surface of the cerebral peduncle?
explanation: Based on your texts, 'The oculomotor nerve (III) emerges from the medial surface of the peduncle'. (Page 65)

text: The trochlear nerve emerges:
explanation: Based on your texts, the trochlear nerves (IV) emerge 'Just below the inferior colliculi', which are located on the dorsal surface of the midbrain. (Page 65)

text: The dorsal surface of the midbrain contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, 'Dorsally, the midbrain has 4 elevations, 2 superior colliculi, & 2 inferior colliculi'. (Page 65)

text: The tectum is located:
explanation: Based on your texts, the midbrain is divided by the cerebral aqueduct into 'a "tectum" dorsally'. (Page 67)

text: The substantia nigra is separated from:
explanation: Based on your texts, the substantia nigra is described as 'separating crus cerebri from the rest of the midbrain'. (Page 67)

text: The basis pedunculi contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, the basis pedunculi 'consists of longitudinal descending fibers... (corticobulbar),... (corticospinal) and... (corticopontine.)'. (Page 67)

text: Which layer of superior colliculus receives optic tract fibers?
explanation: Based on your texts, 'Lamina III or SO, the stratum opticum... consists mainly of axons coming from the optic tract'. (Page 68)

text: The red nucleus is located in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the red nucleus is 'present in the midbrain', specifically within the tegmentum. (Pages 67, 69)

text: Superior cerebellar peduncle decussates at the level of:
explanation: Based on your texts, it is stated that the superior cerebellar peduncle 'decussate at the inferior colliculus'. (Page 69)

text: Dorsal tegmental decussation transmits:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Dorsal tegmental decussation' is explicitly associated with the '(Tectospinal)' tract. (Page 73)

text: The oculomotor nucleus lies around:
explanation: Based on your texts, the oculomotor nucleus 'lies in the central grey matter around the central aqueduct'. (Page 71)

text: The trochlear nucleus is located at the level of:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Trochlear nerve nucleus IV' is located at the 'inferior level' of the midbrain, which is the level of the 'INFERIOR (TECTUM) COLLICULUS'. (Pages 71, 72)

text: Ventral tegmental decussation is for:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Ventral tegmental decussation' is explicitly associated with the '(Rubrospinal)' tract. (Page 73)

text: Superior cerebellar decussation occurs at:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Superior cerebellar decussation' occurs at the level of the 'inferior colliculus'. (Page 69)

text: Motor decussation of pyramids occurs in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'motor decussation' of the pyramidal (corticospinal) tract occurs in the 'Lower level' of the 'closed medulla'. (Page 74)

text: Sensory decussation occurs in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'sensory decussation' occurs in the 'Upper level' of the 'closed medulla'. (Page 74)

text: Tectospinal tract decussates at:
explanation: Based on your texts, the 'Decussation of tectospial tract' occurs in the 'superior level' of the midbrain, which is the level of the superior colliculus. (Page 74)

text: Lateral lemniscus ends in:
explanation: Based on your texts, the lateral lemniscus is described as the tract for the auditory pathway that 'end[s] in auditory temporal cortex areas 41,42'. (Page 75)

text: The largest cells in the cerebral cortex are:
explanation: Based on your texts, Betz cells are specifically identified as 'larger cells (120um)' in the cerebral cortex. (Purkinje cells are large, but are in the cerebellar cortex). (Pages 80, 81)

text: Layer V of cerebral cortex contains:
explanation: Based on your texts, Layer V, the internal pyramidal layer, 'contains large pyramidal neurons' and 'contains Betz cells'. (Page 79)

text: Purkinje cells are found in:
explanation: Based on your texts, Purkinje cells form a distinct layer in the 'cerebellar cortex'. (Page 81)

text: The choroid plexus epithelium is made up of:
explanation: Based on your texts, the choroid plexus epithelium is described as 'a layer of simple cuboidal epithelial cells, known as the ependyma', and these are considered 'modified ependymal cells'. (Page 86)

text: The blood-brain barrier is mainly formed by:
options: Non-fenestrated endothelial cells with tight junctions
explanation: Based on your texts, the blood-brain barrier is characterized by capillaries with 'non-fenestrated endothelial cells held together by tight (occluding) junctions'. (Page 88)

text: Which of the following structures contributes to the blood-CSF barrier?
options: Tight junctions of choroid plexus epithelial cells
explanation: Based on your texts, 'tight junctions' between the epithelial (ependymal) cells of the choroid plexus are responsible for 'making up the blood-CSF barrier'. (Page 87)

text: The dura mater in the cranial cavity consists of:
explanation: Based on your texts, 'Within the cranial cavity, the dura contains two connective tissue sheets: Periosteal layer... and... Meningeal layer'. (Page 90)

text: The subarachnoid space is located:
options: Between dura mater and arachnoid mater
Between arachnoid mater and pia mater
explanation: Based on your texts, 'The space between the arachnoid and the underlying pia mater is called the subarachnoid space'. (Page 32)

text: Which meningeal layer closely follows the gyri and sulci of the brain?
explanation: Based on your texts, the pia mater is 'the only covering to follow the contours of the brain (the gyri and fissures)'. (Page 91)

text: The largest vestibular nucleus is:
explanation: Based on your texts, 'The medial vestibular nucleus: it is the largest nucleus'. (Page 64)

text: Which cells are known to undergo a transition to squamous cells?
Stria vascularis epithelium type is:
explanation: (Page 138).

text: Lens capsule is composed of:
explanation: The lens capsule is 'formed of reticular fibers embedded in a matrix of glycoprotein and sulfated glycosaminoglycans' (Page 110).

text: The ciliary body is continuous posteriorly with:
explanation: The ciliary body is continuous posteriorly with the choroid (Page 103).

text: Contraction of ciliary muscle:
explanation: Contraction of the ciliary muscle fibers pulls the ciliary body forward, decreases tension on the suspensory ligament, and allows the lens to become more convex for near vision (Page 104).

text: Aqueous humor is secreted by:
explanation: The aqueous humor is produced by the non-pigmented ciliary epithelium (pars plicata) of the ciliary processes (Page 109).

text: Bruch's membrane is part of:
explanation: Bruch's membrane is the 4th layer of the choroid, located between the choriocapillaris and the pigment epithelial layer of the retina (Page 106).

text: The highly vascular fenestrated capillary layer of choroid is:
explanation: The capillary layer of the choroid, known as the choriocapillaris, consists of large fenestrated capillaries (Page 106).

text: Bulbar conjunctiva epithelium:
explanation: The bulbar conjunctiva, which covers the sclera, is lined by stratified squamous epithelium (non-keratinized) (Page 120).

text: The sclera forms how much of the fibrous coat of the eyeball?
explanation: The sclera forms the posterior five-sixths (5/6) of the eyeball's outer fibrous tunic (Page 98).

text: The transparent part of the fibrous coat is:
explanation: The transparent cornea is the most anterior part (1/6) of the eye's fibrous coat (Page 99).

text: The corneal epithelium is:
explanation: The corneal epithelium is a stratified squamous (non-cornified) epithelium (Page 99).

text: Bowman's membrane is composed mainly of:
explanation: Bowman's membrane consists of small Type I collagen fibrils (Page 99).

text: Descemet's membrane is secreted by:
explanation: Descemet's membrane corresponds to a thick basal lamina secreted by the corneal endothelium (Page 100).

text: Transparency of cornea is maintained by:
explanation: The transparency of the cornea is due to the uniform diameter and orderly arrangement of its collagen fibers, as well as being avascular (Page 100).

text: The scleral opening where optic nerve fibers pass is called:
explanation: The sclera thins to form a fenestrated membrane called the lamina cribrosa at the point where optic nerve fibers penetrate it (Page 98).

text: Episclera contains:
explanation: The episclera is a sublamina of the sclera that contains vessels and adipose tissue (Page 98).

text: The limbus represents transition between:
explanation: The limbus is the zone of transition between the transparent cornea and the opaque sclera (Page 101).

text: Schlemm's canal is found at:
explanation: The endothelial-lined Schlemm's canal is a characteristic feature found at the limbus (corneo-scleral junction) (Page 101).

text: The pupil is an opening in the:
explanation: The iris is a thin disc that has a central, circular aperture called the pupil (Page 102).

text: Dilator pupillae is derived from:
explanation: The cells of the outer (anterior) layer of the posterior surface of the iris are modified into myoepithelial cells to form the dilator of the iris (dilator pupillae) (Page 102).

text: Sphincter pupillae is located in:
explanation: The sphincter muscle (sphincter pupillae) consists of smooth muscle cells located in the stroma of the iris (Page 102).

text: Eye color depends on:
explanation: The color of the eye (iris) depends on the number of melanocytes in the stroma and the amount of melanin pigment within both the melanocytes and the posterior epithelial layer (Page 103).

text: Accommodation for near vision is due to:
explanation: Accommodation for near vision occurs upon contraction of the ciliary muscle fibers, which allows the lens to become more convex (Page 104).

text: Outer retinal pigment epithelium stores:
explanation: The pigment epithelium of the retina also stores vitamin A, which is a precursor of rhodopsin (Page 113).

text: Retinal detachment occurs between:
explanation: The pigmented epithelial layer is loosely attached to the rods and cones layer (part of the neural retina). A detached retina occurs when the retina separates at this plane (Page 114).

text: Photoreceptor for dim light is:
explanation: The retina has two types of photoreceptors: rods and cones (Page 114). The cones are responsible for 'sharpest color discrimination' (Page 118). This implies the rods, which contain rhodopsin (Page 115), are the photoreceptors for other conditions, such as dim light.

text: Photoreceptor for color vision:
explanation: The fovea centralis consists only of cone photoreceptors and is responsible for 'sharpest color discrimination,' identifying cones as the photoreceptors for color vision (Page 118).

text: The area of greatest visual acuity is:
explanation: The part of the retina directly opposite the center of the lens is the macula lutea. Its center, the fovea centralis, is the area of 'greatest visual acuity' (Page 118).

text: Fovea centralis contains:
explanation: The fovea centralis is devoid of rods and consists 'only of cones photoreceptors' (Page 118).

text: Rhodopsin is present in:
explanation: The outer segment of rod cells contains flattened membranous sacs that contain rhodopsin (Page 115).

text: Iodopsin is present in:
explanation: The visual pigment found in cone cells is iodopsin (Page 116).

text: The outer limiting membrane of retina is formed by:
options: Tight junctions of Muller's cells with photoreceptors
explanation: The external (outer) limiting membrane is formed by junctional complexes between the Muller's cells and the adjacent photoreceptor cells (Page 116).

text: Ganglion cell axons converge at:
explanation: The optic disc (or blind spot) is the site where the optic nerve fibers, which are the axons of the ganglion cells, converge to exit the eye (Page 119).

text: Lens epithelium is present only on:
explanation: A single layer of cuboidal cells (lens epithelium) is present just beneath the capsule on the anterior surface. The posterior capsule has no cells (Page 110).

text: Loss of lens transparency is called:
explanation: A cataract is defined as the loss of lens transparency (Page 110).

text: Presbyopia is due to:
explanation: Presbyopia is defined as the loss of lens elasticity (Page 110).

text: Hyaloid canal represents:
explanation: The hyaloid canal represents the site of the embryonic hyaloid artery (Page 111).

text: The vitreous body contains mainly:
explanation: The vitreous body contains 99% water, hyaluronic acid, and thin fibrils of collagen, specifically Type II and Type XI (Page 111).

text: Aqueous humor drains via:
explanation: Aqueous humor exits the anterior chamber through the trabecular meshwork and is collected in the canal of Schlemm (Page 109).

text: Meibomian glands are:
explanation: The Tarsal (Meibomian) glands are described as long sebaceous glands (Page 120).

text: Zeis glands are associated with:
explanation: The glands of Zeis are small sebaceous glands that empty into the follicles of the eyelashes (Page 120).

text: Moll's glands are:
explanation: The glands of Moll are described as small apocrine sweat glands (Page 120).

text: Lacrimal gland type is:
explanation: The lacrimal gland is a compound tubuloalveolar gland with acini that are 'pure serous' (Page 121).

text: Epithelium of lacrimal sac and nasolacrimal duct:
explanation: Both the lacrimal sac and the nasolacrimal duct are lined by pseudostratified columnar epithelium (Page 121).

text: Palpebral conjunctiva epithelium:
explanation: The palpebral conjunctiva is lined by stratified columnar epithelium that contains numerous goblet cells (Page 120).

text: Main tear drainage structure:
explanation: Tears are drained via the lacrimal canaliculi, which lead to the lacrimal sac, and then into the nasolacrimal duct (Page 121).

text: The conjunctiva covering sclera is:
explanation: The bulbar conjunctiva is the part of the conjunctiva that covers the exposed part of the sclera (Page 120).

text: Corneal sensitivity is due to:
options: Free nerve endings in corneal epithelium
explanation: The corneal epithelium is very sensitive because it contains many free nerve endings (Page 99).

text: The auricle (pinna) is mainly composed of:
explanation: The auricle (pinna) of the external ear consists of a plate of elastic cartilage (Page 123).

text: Ceruminous glands are:
explanation: Ceruminous glands, which produce earwax, are modified apocrine sweat glands (Page 123).

text: The external auditory meatus is lined by:
explanation: The external auditory meatus is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Page 123).

text: The outer third of the external auditory canal is:
explanation: The outer 1/3 of the external auditory meatus is cartilaginous (Page 123).

text: Tympanic membrane outer surface is lined by:
explanation: The outer surface of the tympanic membrane is lined by keratinized stratified squamous epithelium (Page 123).

text: Tympanic membrane middle layer is formed of:
explanation: The middle layer of the tympanic membrane is formed of dense connective tissue, with collagen fibers arranged into outer radial and inner circular layers (Page 123).

text: The inner surface of the tympanic membrane is lined by:
explanation: The inner surface of the tympanic membrane is lined by simple cuboidal epithelium (Page 123).

text: The three auditory ossicles are:
explanation: The three auditory ossicles are the Malleus (hammer), Incus (anvil), and Stapes (stirrup) (Page 124).

text: The auditory ossicles are connected by:
explanation: The auditory ossicles (malleus, incus, and stapes) are connected by synovial joints (Page 124).

text: The fluid inside the membranous labyrinth is:
explanation: The membranous labyrinth is a system of canals and sacs that contains endolymph (Page 124).

text: Type I hair cells are:
explanation: The Type I hair cells found in the maculae and cristae ampullaris are flask-shaped (Page 125).

text: Kinocilium in maculae is:
explanation: Each hair cell in the maculae has stereocilia and one kinocilium, which is described as a non-motile cilium (Page 125).

text: Cupula of semicircular canal contains:
explanation: The cupula, found in the crista ampullaris of the semicircular canals, is a gelatinous glycoprotein mass that does not contain otoliths (Page 126).

text: Scala media is filled with:
explanation: The scala media (or cochlear duct) is filled with endolymph (Page 126).

text: The organ of Corti rests on:
explanation: The Organ of Corti, which is the sensory receptor for hearing, rests on the basilar membrane (Page 127).

text: Pillar cells form:
explanation: The Pillar cells (inner and outer) are tall columnar cells that form the boundaries of the inner tunnel, also known as the Tunnel of Corti (Page 127).

text: Inner hair cells form:
explanation: The inner hair cells are arranged in one row (Page 128).

text: Outer hair cells form:
explanation: The outer hair cells are arranged in 3-4 rows (Page 128).

text: Stereocilia arrangement of outer hair cells is:
explanation: The microvilli (stereocilia) of the outer hair cells are arranged in a V-shape (Page 128).

text: Tectorial membrane is:
explanation: The tectorial membrane is described as an acellular, gelatinous structure (Page 128).

text: The sensory receptor for hearing is:
explanation: The Organ of Corti is the sensory receptor for hearing (Page 127).

text: Spiral ganglion neurons are:
explanation: The spiral ganglion is formed of bipolar neurons (Page 129).

text: Which part of the ear contains the cochlea?
explanation: The cochlea is a component of the bony labyrinth, which is part of the inner ear (Page 124).

text: What structure do the tips of the microvilli of hair cells contact?
explanation: The tips of the tallest microvilli (stereocilia) of the outer hair cells are in contact with the tectorial membrane (Page 128).

text: Which cells are responsible for supporting the outer hair cells?
explanation: The Phalangeal cells (also known as Deiters' cells) are the supporting cells for the outer hair cells (Page 127).

text: What is the shape of the inner hair cells?
explanation: The inner hair cells are described as flask-shaped (piriform) (Page 128).

text: Which type of cell forms the outer edge of the Organ of Corti?
explanation: The cells of Claudius are cuboidal cells that form the outer edge of the Organ of Corti (Page 128).

text: Where are the mitochondria primarily located in the hair cells?
explanation: In both inner and outer hair cells, abundant mitochondria are located at the base of the cell (Page 128).

text: What type of nerve endings are associated with the outer hair cells?
explanation: Both afferent and efferent nerve endings are associated with the base of the outer hair cells (Page 128).

text: What is the primary structural feature of the outer hair cells?
explanation: A key structural feature of the outer hair cells is that their microvilli (stereocilia) are arranged in a V-shape (Page 128).

text: Otic vesicle gives rise to:
explanation: The epithelium of the inner ear is derived from the otic vesicle (Page 123).
